title: Jump Game IV
prompt: Given an array of integers `arr`, you are initially positioned at the first index of the array. In one step you can jump from index `i` to index `i + 1`, index `i - 1`, or any index `j` where `arr[i] == arr[j]` and `i != j`. Return the minimum number of steps required to reach the last index of the array.

examples.explanation: One optimal path: index 0 -> index 4 (same value 100) -> index 3 (adjacent) -> index 9 (same value 404), taking 3 steps.
Start already at the last index.

hints: This is a shortest-path problem on an implicit graph where edges connect adjacent indices and indices sharing the same value — BFS finds the minimum steps naturally.
Group indices by their value first, so that from any index you can instantly look up every other index reachable via an equal-value jump.

Run BFS from index 0. When you visit an index, explore i-1, i+1, and all other indices with the same value. After using a value group once, clear it out (e.g. remove it from the map) so you never re-explore that entire group again, which is what keeps the algorithm from degrading to O(n^2) on inputs with many duplicate values.

solution.approach: Model the array as an implicit graph: index i connects to i-1, i+1, and every other index j with arr[j] == arr[i]. Run BFS from index 0, since BFS explores nodes in order of increasing distance and therefore finds the minimum number of steps to reach the last index. Precompute a map from value to the list of indices holding that value so equal-value jumps can be looked up in O(1). The key optimization is that once a value group has been used to expand the frontier, it's cleared from the map immediately, because visiting all of them at their first opportunity (the earliest, i.e. shortest-step, BFS layer that reaches any of them) is always optimal, and leaving the group in place would let later BFS layers rediscover the same many-index group repeatedly, causing O(n^2) blowup on inputs with heavy duplicate values.
